cases.output:
You are a meticulous evidence reader for Tayyari, a career-intelligence product. You read ONE source about a person
and extract only what that source actually evidences. A senior synthesizer will merge your output with other readers'
outputs into a skill graph, so precision matters far more than coverage.

This source is a RESUME.
- Capture every role: title, employer, dates, and the concrete outcomes in its bullets (numbers, scale, ownership).
- Fill "person": full name, the most recent title as currentRole (students: e.g. "CS Student"), city, and yearsExperience =
  full-time professional experience computed from the dates up to today, to one decimal place. Exclude internships,
  student clubs and part-time study jobs; count freelance only when it was their main work. Students: 0.
- Separate skills that are merely LISTED in a skills section (strength 1–2) from skills that are USED in an
  experience or project bullet (strength 3+). Leadership, mentoring, ownership and collaboration count as skills too.
- Typical improvement notes: impact described but not measured, strong projects missing from the resume, vague bullets,
  missing links to GitHub or live work, skills listed without any evidence.
- "sub" counts what the resume holds, e.g. "6 roles · 23 skills".

Rules:
- Evidence only. Never infer a skill the source does not show. Never invent employers, repos, numbers or dates.
- Be specific: name the repo, project, employer, case study or page in every evidence sentence; keep real numbers.
- Calibrate strength with the 1–5 rubric in the schema; listing a technology is not using it.
- No flattery and no adjectives like "impressive" or "passionate". Plain, factual language.
- Notes must be concrete and actionable, and at least one must be an honest improvement opportunity for THIS source.
- Respect the length limits written in the schema descriptions (characters, list sizes).
- If the source is empty, broken or unreadable, say so in "summary", return what little you can, and keep lists short.
- If the text is missing and the original file is attached to the message, read the attached document.
- Respond ONLY through the structured output. No prose outside it.

RIYA KAPOOR
Frontend Engineer · Bengaluru, India
riya.kapoor.dev@example.com · github.com/riyakapoor · riyakapoor.design

SUMMARY
Frontend engineer with 2.4 years of experience building fast, accessible commerce interfaces in React and TypeScript.
I care about motion, design systems and the details that make a product feel finished. Currently on the storefront
team at Kitebird, a D2C home-goods brand, where I own checkout and the shared component library.

EXPERIENCE

Kitebird — Frontend Engineer II                                              Bengaluru · Jul 2025 – Present
D2C commerce startup (home goods), ~40 engineers, storefront + mobile web.
- Rebuilt the three-step checkout as a single-page flow in React and TypeScript with optimistic cart updates;
  checkout conversion rose 9.4% in the A/B test and LCP on the payment step dropped from 4.1s to 1.9s.
- Own Kite UI, the shared React component library (42 components, typed tokens, Storybook docs) used by 3 product squads.
- Led the storefront migration to React 18 and Vite, removing the legacy CRA build and cutting local build times.
- Ran a WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility audit of checkout with design and fixed the critical issues (focus order, labels,
  colour contrast, screen-reader announcements for cart updates).
- Review pull requests for the 4-person web team and pair with designers on Figma-to-code handoffs.
- Mentored 2 frontend interns through their 6-month internships; both received full-time offers.

Kitebird — Frontend Engineer                                                  Bengaluru · May 2024 – Jun 2025
- Built the backend-for-frontend (Node.js, Express) for the mobile web app, aggregating catalog, pricing and
  inventory APIs into one typed endpoint per screen.
- Owned API contracts with 2 backend teams (REST and a GraphQL catalog service) and wrote the client-side data layer.
- Set up preview deployments for every pull request with GitHub Actions and Vercel.
- Shipped the product-detail page redesign, including image galleries, variant pickers and delivery-date estimates.
- Partnered with the PM and design lead on checkout research; joined 6 usability sessions and turned findings into tickets.
- Wrote internal docs on motion guidelines and component usage for the web team.

Saffron Ledger — Frontend Engineering Intern                                  Bengaluru · Jan 2024 – Apr 2024
Fintech startup building bookkeeping software for small businesses.
- Built dashboard widgets (cash-flow charts, invoice tables) in React with TypeScript and Recharts.
- Created a small Figma-backed component kit for the dashboard, later adopted for the whole web app.
- Fixed table rendering performance for accounts with 10,000+ invoices using virtualised lists.

Freelance — UI Developer                                                       Remote · Jun 2023 – Dec 2023
- Designed and built marketing sites and a component kit for 3 early-stage clients (Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Figma).
- Delivered responsive, animated landing pages and handed over a reusable design system to each client.

Google Developer Student Club, Nandi Institute of Technology — Web Lead         Bengaluru · 2022 – 2023
- Ran weekly React workshops for 60+ students and organised a 24-hour campus hackathon.

Open source — Maintainer, motion-kit                                           2023 – Present
- Maintain motion-kit, a spring-physics animation library for React (212 GitHub stars), and review community PRs.

PROJECTS
- motion-kit — Spring-physics animation primitives for React with gesture support and reduced-motion handling.
  TypeScript, Vitest, GitHub Actions. github.com/riyakapoor/motion-kit
- checkout-lab — Experiments in checkout UX: optimistic updates, address autocomplete, skeleton states. Next.js.
- design-tokens — A Style Dictionary pipeline that turns Figma variables into CSS, TypeScript and Tailwind tokens.
- Kite UI docs — Public Storybook for Kitebird's component library (internal repo, public docs site).

SKILLS
Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Python (basic), Go (basic)
Frontend: React, Next.js, Framer Motion, Tailwind CSS, Storybook, Recharts, Redux Toolkit, TanStack Query
Backend: Node.js, Express, tRPC, REST, GraphQL, PostgreSQL, Prisma
Tooling: Vite, Vitest, Jest, GitHub Actions, Vercel, Git
Design: Figma, design systems, motion design, accessibility (WCAG 2.1)
Ways of working: code review, mentoring, technical writing, working with PM and design

EDUCATION
B.Tech, Computer Science and Engineering — Nandi Institute of Technology, Bengaluru          2020 – 2024
CGPA 8.6 / 10. Final-year project: a real-time collaborative whiteboard in React and WebSockets.

ACHIEVEMENTS
- Kitebird "Ship It" award, H1 2025, for the checkout rebuild.
- Speaker, ReactFoo Bengaluru community meetup (2025): "Springs, not durations — motion that feels physical".

Lovable badge: "Edit with Lovable" present

- React + Vite (Lovable default stack)
- Tailwind CSS

- lucide-react icons

- No error-monitoring script detected

## Landing page (visible text)
Hero: "Dinner, sorted. From whatever's in your fridge."
Sub: "Add what you have. Recipe Genie suggests three recipes you can actually cook tonight — with swaps for what's missing."
Primary button: "Try it free" · Secondary: "See an example"
Social proof line: "Loved by 600+ home cooks"
Feature cards:
- "Pantry in seconds" — type or paste your ingredients; Genie understands "half an onion" and "leftover rice".
- "Three good options" — quick, comfort, or healthy, each with time, difficulty and a shopping gap list.
- "Swap anything" — no cream? Genie rewrites the step with what you have.
- "Save your favourites" — keep the recipes that worked and rate them.
Footer: "Made by Riya Kapoor · riyakapoor.design · Built with Lovable"

## App screens and user flows
Flow 1 — Sign in: email magic link (Supabase auth). Empty state after sign-in: "Your pantry is empty. Add 3+ ingredients to start."
Flow 2 — Generate: pantry input with chips → "Ask the Genie" button → loading state with rotating messages
("Checking the spice rack…") → three recipe cards (Quick / Comfort / Healthy) with time, difficulty and "missing: 2 items".
Recipe detail: ingredients, numbered steps, "Swap an ingredient" dialog that regenerates one step.
Flow 3 — Save & share: heart to save into Favourites; public share link per recipe (/r/:id) with Open Graph preview.

## Prompt-driven UI notes
- The generate screen shows the dietary preferences that are sent with the prompt (vegetarian, no nuts, under 30 min).
- Recipes come back as structured JSON rendered into cards (fields: title, time, difficulty, ingredients, steps, swaps).
- Regenerate button on each card; no visible rating of output quality beyond the favourite heart.
- Error state: a toast "The Genie is tired, try again" when generation fails; no retry with backoff.

## Other observations from the page
- Settings page: dietary preferences and units (metric/imperial). No onboarding tour.
- No privacy policy or terms page linked.
- Lighthouse-style signals: images are lazy-loaded; the landing page ships ~410 KB of JS.

"I build interfaces that feel physical — springs, not durations." Frontend engineer at Kitebird in Bengaluru.

## Case study 1 — "Checkout, rebuilt" (Kitebird, 2025)
Role: lead frontend engineer, with one designer and one PM.
Problem: a three-step checkout with a 4.1s LCP on the payment step and a high drop-off at the address form.
Process: joined 6 usability sessions, mapped drop-off points, prototyped a single-page checkout in Figma and code,
shipped behind a feature flag, ran an A/B test for 3 weeks.

Audited checkout against WCAG 2.1 AA with the design lead: 37 issues logged, 21 fixed in two sprints
(focus order, form labels, contrast, live-region announcements for cart updates). Describes testing with NVDA and

## Case study 3 — "Kite UI: a design system for a four-person team" (Kitebird, 2024–2025)
42 components, tokens generated from Figma variables via the design-tokens pipeline, Storybook docs,
adoption by 3 product squads. Explains the trade-offs of headless primitives vs styled components.
Mentions typing the whole package in strict TypeScript.

## Case study 4 — "motion-kit: designing with springs" (open source)
Why springs beat duration-based easing, the API design of useSpring/usePresence, gesture handoff, and how the

a Figma-backed component kit later adopted across the web app. Outcome not quantified.

- "Springs, not durations" (2025) — essay version of her ReactFoo meetup talk.

- Outcomes are present but usually appear below the fold, after the process narrative.

cases.name: SYNTH_SYSTEM
cases.output:
You are a senior engineering hiring manager and career strategist who has hired and coached hundreds of
engineers, designers and product people. Several reader agents have each read one source about ONE person (resume, GitHub,
Lovable apps, portfolio, other links, their own notes). Merge their evidence into a calibrated, honest skill graph of the
person's CURRENT role, and map the most probable NEXT roles. Your output is rendered as an interactive constellation and a
career map, and every number will be scrutinised by the person — so be calibrated, specific and grounded.

1. The person
- Use their real name if any source states it; otherwise "You".
- currentRole = their most recent title, normalised: drop levels and grades ("Frontend Engineer II", "SDE-2" →
  "Frontend Engineer", "Software Engineer"). Students → e.g. "CS Student"; career switchers → the role they hold today.
- yearsExperience = full-time professional years up to today (internships excluded), one decimal.
- headline = "<Current role> · <N.N> yrs · <City>" (omit parts you do not know).

2. Domains (4–7), ordered by relevance to the CURRENT role
- Domains are the areas a hiring manager would assess for this role and its neighbours (e.g. Frontend Engineering,
  Product & Design, Backend & APIs, AI & LLM Apps, Engineering Practice, Collaboration).
- short ≤ 16 characters. Domain score = importance-weighted blend of its skills, not a plain average.

3. Skills (12–26 total, 2–5 per domain)
- Scoring rubric, apply it strictly:
    90–100  multiple strong public artifacts AND professional depth (e.g. a library with real adoption + shipped at work)
    75–89   solid professional evidence (owned or shipped it at work, with outcomes)
    60–74   working proficiency (used repeatedly in projects or at work, without standout proof)
    40–59   some exposure (listed, used once, or a small/personal project only)
    under 40  little or no evidence — a GAP
- Self-reported claims (notes, a skills list) without corroboration cap at ~55. Corroboration across sources raises
  confidence; contradictions lower it.
- INCLUDE 3–6 GAP skills (score < 45) that matter for their most probable next roles (and their goal, if given), so the
  graph shows where to grow. A gap's evidence states the observed absence ("No eval harness in any of 34 repos").
- evidence: 1–3 items. sourceId MUST be one of the listed source ids. Text ≤ 90 characters, naming the repo / project /
  role / page. NEVER invent employers, repos, metrics or dates — only use what the readers reported.
- unlocks: exact titles from your roles list that this skill opens or strengthens (0–3).
- Skill names ≤ 22 characters; ids are kebab-case and unique across the whole graph (domains and skills included).

4. Next roles (4–6)
- The most probable next roles branching from the current role: the natural step up (e.g. "Senior Frontend Engineer"),
  adjacent lateral moves their evidence supports, and a stretch role. If the person stated a goal, the goal role MUST be
  one of them, even if alignment is low — be honest about the distance.
- alignment = honest, importance-weighted coverage of that role's requirements today (roughly the weighted mean of
  min(current / target, 1)), as an integer 0–100. Do not inflate; 85+ means they could interview for it now.
- eta = realistic time to become hireable for it at ~6 hours/week ("~4 months", "~1 year").
- why ≤ 160 characters, grounded in named evidence: why this role fits AND what stands between them and it.
- requirements: 4–7 per role, mixing strengths they already have (have = true, current ≥ 60) and gaps with realistic
  targets. When a requirement maps to a skill on the graph, reuse its exact name, set skillId to that skill's id, and set
  current to that skill's score. Requirements that are not on the graph (e.g. "System design") still get an honest current.
- Titles ≤ 26 characters.

5. Mastery
- score = how complete they are for their CURRENT role at their level of experience (a 2-year engineer is judged against
  a 2-year bar, not a staff bar).

# Recipe Genie â€” dinner from whatever is in your fridge

URL: https://recipe-genie.lovable.app
Description: Tell Recipe Genie what's in your kitchen and get three recipes you can cook tonight. Built with Lovable.
Built with: Lovable (Vite + React)
Lovable badge: "Edit with Lovable" present
Linked GitHub repository: github.com/riyakapoor/recipe-genie-web

## Libraries and services detected
- React + Vite (Lovable default stack)
- Tailwind CSS
- shadcn/ui components (Radix primitives: dialog, tabs, toast, dropdown-menu)
- Supabase JS client: email magic-link auth, Postgres tables via REST (recipes, pantry_items, favourites)
- OpenAI API (chat completions) called from a Supabase Edge Function `generate-recipes`
- lucide-react icons
- No analytics or product-tracking script detected (no GA, PostHog, Plausible, Mixpanel)
- No error-monitoring script detected

## Landing page (visible text)
Hero: "Dinner, sorted. From whatever's in your fridge."
Sub: "Add what you have. Recipe Genie suggests three recipes you can actually cook tonight â€” with swaps for what's missing."
Primary button: "Try it free" Â· Secondary: "See an example"
Social proof line: "Loved by 600+ home cooks"
Feature cards:
- "Pantry in seconds" â€” type or paste your ingredients; Genie understands "half an onion" and "leftover rice".
- "Three good options" â€” quick, comfort, or healthy, each with time, difficulty and a shopping gap list.
- "Swap anything" â€” no cream? Genie rewrites the step with what you have.
- "Save your favourites" â€” keep the recipes that worked and rate them.
Footer: "Made by Riya Kapoor Â· riyakapoor.design Â· Built with Lovable"

## App screens and user flows
Flow 1 â€” Sign in: email magic link (Supabase auth). Empty state after sign-in: "Your pantry is empty. Add 3+ ingredients to start."
Flow 2 â€” Generate: pantry input with chips â†’ "Ask the Genie" button â†’ loading state with rotating messages
("Checking the spice rackâ€¦") â†’ three recipe cards (Quick / Comfort / Healthy) with time, difficulty and "missing: 2 items".
Recipe detail: ingredients, numbered steps, "Swap an ingredient" dialog that regenerates one step.
Flow 3 â€” Save & share: heart to save into Favourites; public share link per recipe (/r/:id) with Open Graph preview.

## Prompt-driven UI notes
- The generate screen shows the dietary preferences that are sent with the prompt (vegetarian, no nuts, under 30 min).
- Recipes come back as structured JSON rendered into cards (fields: title, time, difficulty, ingredients, steps, swaps).
- Regenerate button on each card; no visible rating of output quality beyond the favourite heart.
- Error state: a toast "The Genie is tired, try again" when generation fails; no retry with backoff.

## Other observations from the page
- Settings page: dietary preferences and units (metric/imperial). No onboarding tour.
- No privacy policy or terms page linked.
- Lighthouse-style signals: images are lazy-loaded; the landing page ships ~410 KB of JS.

"I build interfaces that feel physical â€” springs, not durations." Frontend engineer at Kitebird in Bengaluru.
Selected work (5 case studies), two essays on motion design, and a link to GitHub. Large animated hero with a
spring-driven cursor trail (respects prefers-reduced-motion). No mention of AI or LLM work anywhere on the site.

## About
Frontend engineer, 2.4 years. Previously interned at Saffron Ledger (fintech dashboards) and freelanced for early-stage
startups. "My favourite work sits between design and engineering: design systems, motion, and the last 10% of polish."
Tools listed: React, TypeScript, Framer Motion, Figma, Storybook, Tailwind.

## Case study 1 â€” "Checkout, rebuilt" (Kitebird, 2025)
Role: lead frontend engineer, with one designer and one PM.
Problem: a three-step checkout with a 4.1s LCP on the payment step and a high drop-off at the address form.
Process: joined 6 usability sessions, mapped drop-off points, prototyped a single-page checkout in Figma and code,
shipped behind a feature flag, ran an A/B test for 3 weeks.
Outcome (stated near the end of the page): +9.4% checkout conversion, LCP 1.9s on the payment step.
Includes motion specs for the cart drawer and address autocomplete, and before/after screen recordings.

## Case study 2 â€” "An accessibility audit that actually shipped" (Kitebird, 2025)
Audited checkout against WCAG 2.1 AA with the design lead: 37 issues logged, 21 fixed in two sprints
(focus order, form labels, contrast, live-region announcements for cart updates). Describes testing with NVDA and
VoiceOver by hand. Notes that automated checks (axe) are "next on the list" â€” not yet in CI.

## Case study 3 â€” "Kite UI: a design system for a four-person team" (Kitebird, 2024â€“2025)
42 components, tokens generated from Figma variables via the design-tokens pipeline, Storybook docs,
adoption by 3 product squads. Explains the trade-offs of headless primitives vs styled components.
Mentions typing the whole package in strict TypeScript.

## Case study 4 â€” "motion-kit: designing with springs" (open source)
Why springs beat duration-based easing, the API design of useSpring/usePresence, gesture handoff, and how the
library reached 212 GitHub stars. Embedded interactive demos.

## Case study 5 â€” "Saffron Ledger dashboard" (internship, 2024)
Cash-flow charts and invoice tables for small-business bookkeeping; virtualised lists for 10,000+ invoices;
a Figma-backed component kit later adopted across the web app. Outcome not quantified.

## Writing
- "Springs, not durations" (2025) â€” essay version of her ReactFoo meetup talk.
- "Motion budgets: how much animation is too much?" (2024).

## Observations
- Strong visual craft; every case study has motion specs or interactive demos.
- Outcomes are present but usually appear below the fold, after the process narrative.
- Recipe Genie and notes-ai (AI projects) are not featured.
- No contact form; email link only. Site built with Next.js and Framer Motion, deployed on Vercel.

# Recipe Genie â€” dinner from whatever is in your fridge

URL: https://recipe-genie.lovable.app
Description: Tell Recipe Genie what's in your kitchen and get three recipes you can cook tonight. Built with Lovable.
Built with: Lovable (Vite + React)
Lovable badge: "Edit with Lovable" present
Linked GitHub repository: github.com/riyakapoor/recipe-genie-web

## Libraries and services detected
- React + Vite (Lovable default stack)
- Tailwind CSS
- shadcn/ui components (Radix primitives: dialog, tabs, toast, dropdown-menu)
- Supabase JS client: email magic-link auth, Postgres tables via REST (recipes, pantry_items, favourites)
- OpenAI API (chat completions) called from a Supabase Edge Function `generate-recipes`
- lucide-react icons
- No analytics or product-tracking script detected (no GA, PostHog, Plausible, Mixpanel)
- No error-monitoring script detected

## Landing page (visible text)
Hero: "Dinner, sorted. From whatever's in your fridge."
Sub: "Add what you have. Recipe Genie suggests three recipes you can actually cook tonight â€” with swaps for what's missing."
Primary button: "Try it free" Â· Secondary: "See an example"
Social proof line: "Loved by 600+ home cooks"
Feature cards:
- "Pantry in seconds" â€” type or paste your ingredients; Genie understands "half an onion" and "leftover rice".
- "Three good options" â€” quick, comfort, or healthy, each with time, difficulty and a shopping gap list.
- "Swap anything" â€” no cream? Genie rewrites the step with what you have.
- "Save your favourites" â€” keep the recipes that worked and rate them.
Footer: "Made by Riya Kapoor Â· riyakapoor.design Â· Built with Lovable"

## App screens and user flows
Flow 1 â€” Sign in: email magic link (Supabase auth). Empty state after sign-in: "Your pantry is empty. Add 3+ ingredients to start."
Flow 2 â€” Generate: pantry input with chips â†’ "Ask the Genie" button â†’ loading state with rotating messages
("Checking the spice rackâ€¦") â†’ three recipe cards (Quick / Comfort / Healthy) with time, difficulty and "missing: 2 items".
Recipe detail: ingredients, numbered steps, "Swap an ingredient" dialog that regenerates one step.
Flow 3 â€” Save & share: heart to save into Favourites; public share link per recipe (/r/:id) with Open Graph preview.

## Prompt-driven UI notes
- The generate screen shows the dietary preferences that are sent with the prompt (vegetarian, no nuts, under 30 min).
- Recipes come back as structured JSON rendered into cards (fields: title, time, difficulty, ingredients, steps, swaps).
- Regenerate button on each card; no visible rating of output quality beyond the favourite heart.
- Error state: a toast "The Genie is tired, try again" when generation fails; no retry with backoff.

## Other observations from the page
- Settings page: dietary preferences and units (metric/imperial). No onboarding tour.
- No privacy policy or terms page linked.
- Lighthouse-style signals: images are lazy-loaded; the landing page ships ~410 KB of JS.

## Home
"I build interfaces that feel physical â€” springs, not durations." Frontend engineer at Kitebird in Bengaluru.
Selected work (5 case studies), two essays on motion design, and a link to GitHub. Large animated hero with a
spring-driven cursor trail (respects prefers-reduced-motion). No mention of AI or LLM work anywhere on the site.

## About
Frontend engineer, 2.4 years. Previously interned at Saffron Ledger (fintech dashboards) and freelanced for early-stage
startups. "My favourite work sits between design and engineering: design systems, motion, and the last 10% of polish."
Tools listed: React, TypeScript, Framer Motion, Figma, Storybook, Tailwind.

## Case study 1 â€” "Checkout, rebuilt" (Kitebird, 2025)
Role: lead frontend engineer, with one designer and one PM.
Problem: a three-step checkout with a 4.1s LCP on the payment step and a high drop-off at the address form.
Process: joined 6 usability sessions, mapped drop-off points, prototyped a single-page checkout in Figma and code,
shipped behind a feature flag, ran an A/B test for 3 weeks.
Outcome (stated near the end of the page): +9.4% checkout conversion, LCP 1.9s on the payment step.
Includes motion specs for the cart drawer and address autocomplete, and before/after screen recordings.

## Case study 2 â€” "An accessibility audit that actually shipped" (Kitebird, 2025)
Audited checkout against WCAG 2.1 AA with the design lead: 37 issues logged, 21 fixed in two sprints
(focus order, form labels, contrast, live-region announcements for cart updates). Describes testing with NVDA and
VoiceOver by hand. Notes that automated checks (axe) are "next on the list" â€” not yet in CI.

## Case study 3 â€” "Kite UI: a design system for a four-person team" (Kitebird, 2024â€“2025)
42 components, tokens generated from Figma variables via the design-tokens pipeline, Storybook docs,
adoption by 3 product squads. Explains the trade-offs of headless primitives vs styled components.
Mentions typing the whole package in strict TypeScript.

## Case study 4 â€” "motion-kit: designing with springs" (open source)
Why springs beat duration-based easing, the API design of useSpring/usePresence, gesture handoff, and how the
library reached 212 GitHub stars. Embedded interactive demos.

## Case study 5 â€” "Saffron Ledger dashboard" (internship, 2024)
Cash-flow charts and invoice tables for small-business bookkeeping; virtualised lists for 10,000+ invoices;
a Figma-backed component kit later adopted across the web app. Outcome not quantified.

## Writing
- "Springs, not durations" (2025) â€” essay version of her ReactFoo meetup talk.
- "Motion budgets: how much animation is too much?" (2024).

## Observations
- Strong visual craft; every case study has motion specs or interactive demos.
- Outcomes are present but usually appear below the fold, after the process narrative.
- Recipe Genie and notes-ai (AI projects) are not featured.
- No contact form; email link only. Site built with Next.js and Framer Motion, deployed on Vercel.
